Here are is the full contingency table, for those who want more details. Gender is ♀/♂︎/? and trans identity is → (cis), ⚧ (trans), or ? (no response).

<pre> 2018 → ⚧ ? ♀ 26 19 4 49 ♂︎ 1034 2 83 1119 ? 19 14 160 193 1079 35 247 1361 2019 → ⚧ ? ♀ 16 16 0 32 ♂︎ 1071 1 28 1100 ? 19 11 49 79 1106 28 77 1211 2020 → ⚧ ? ♀ 12 21 1 34 ♂︎ 1124 2 73 1199 ? 23 15 77 115 1159 38 151 1348 Total → ⚧ ? ♀ 54 56 5 115 ♂︎ 3229 5 184 3418 ? 61 40 286 387 3344 101 475 3920 </pre>

I have a few nitpicks about Taylor's statistics:

  • Your totals include non-responses. I think it would be better to only include people who responded to both gender and trans identity

  • The huge male bias in the sample makes it really hard to compare to general populations. In particular, observing that 51% of women are trans is not meaningful since trans people are 91% male.

  • The Williams study you site doesn't break down the statistics by gender, so we can't compare cis-women:trans-women directly. The overall % trans in this data is 1.8%, but even this isn't comparable to 0.58% since trans-men probably outnumber trans-women (NYT suggests 65% trans-men).

  • Haskell programmers have a ton of socioeconomic factors that might correlate with gender identity (age, location, etc).

replies.text: Thanks! I at least edited the post to not count non-responses (and credit your comment for pointing out the oversight). For a moment I was worried that our totals weren't matching up (e.g., I read your table to say that in 2020, you think 12+21+1124+2 = 1159 people answered both questions, whereas I got 1192), but it looks like that's just because you're counting the "Non-binary" responses in the "?" row (1192 − 1159 = 33, and there were 33 "Non-binary" responses in 2020).
